title: The Italian Wine Pop Quiz
summary:
See All of Our Monthly Italian Wine Pop Quiz Questions

The post The Italian Wine Pop Quiz appeared first on Opening a Bottle.
content:
< 1 min read

Each month in my newsletter, I have been sending readers a trivia question about Italian wine. See all of these questions below and see how you do. I’ll try to add some more advanced functionality at a later date.

&&&

The Married Vines of Umbria

The practice of training vines into trees in Umbria — known as vite maritata — was pioneered by which ancient people?

CORRECT.

Etruscans are often credited with this practice which was widespread up until the post World War II years, when more volume-oriented practices were adopted. But to this day, as I discovered, you can find examples of this ancient practice at select farms in the rural countryside.

INCORRECT.

By the time the Romans arrived, viticulture via married vines was already well established in Umbria.

INCORRECT.

While the Celts were largely to the north, they did have some linguistic and cultural influences on Umbria. But those influences did not pertain so much to the vine.

INCORRECT.

While the ancient Umbri people do give this region its name, it was their chief rival — who pushed them to the east side of the Tevere River — who is largely given credit for establishing viticulture.

Chardonnay in Italy

Chardonnay is the eighth most widely planted wine grape in Italy, ahead of Moscato Bianco, Garganega, Fiano and many more darlings of the white wine renaissance. Chardonnay’s economic resilience is tied to both still and sparkling wines. So ... which region has the most plantings of Chardonnay?

CORRECT.

Veneto is a colossus when it comes to total vineyard acreage, and is second only to Sicily in terms of the most land under vine in Italy. It is perhaps no surprise then that Chardonnay is a key grape in Veneto’s mix, accounting for roughly 5,000 of the region’s 103,000 total hectares. Although Glera, the backbone of Prosecco, has 8 times more vineyard coverage in the region.

INCORRECT.

Of all 20 Italian wine regions, Trentino-Alto Adige probably places the most importance on Chardonnay. It is a vital player in Trentodoc sparkling wines, and Alto Adige’s producers swear by its versatility in their vineyards. By recent estimates, there are between 3,400 and 3,500 hectares planted in this region — a good chunk, but not the most.

INCORRECT.

Lombardy has certainly embraced Chardonnay, particularly in the wine region of Franciacorta, which many believe is Italy’s answer to Champagne (I think Trentodoc and Alta Langa make just as strong a case). However, Chardonnay only makes up 13% of Lombardy’s 23,400 hectares. Not enough to put it No. 1.

INCORRECT.

Sicily trails the leading region by just a few hectares. If you are thinking, wait, Chardonnay is a cool-climate grape. What’s it doing in Sicily? I share your curiosity. However, the high elevations of Etna give Chardonnay a long growing season, and many of Sicily’s legacy wineries — Planeta, Donnafugata and Tasca d’Almerita, to name three — have long seen it as a way to prove Sicily’s white wine bona fides internationally.

Aeolian Islands Viticulture

The Aeolian Islands off of Sicily’s northeastern coast are best know for white and sweet wines made from Malvasia delle Lipari. Which island has the most land planted under vine?

CORRECT.

The island of Salina has between 70 and 80 hectares of land planted to grapevines for mostly wine production, yet the entire Aeolian Islands only has 115 to 120 hectares. So why is the grape not called Malvasia delle Salina? The best theory has to do with Lipari’s significance as the main commercial port of the archipelago.

INCORRECT.

Vulcano’s spares landscape is defined by thermal vents, mud baths and calderas. Less than 10 hectares are occupied by the vine.

INCORRECT.

Lipari is home to between 80 and 90 percent of the population of the entire Aeolian Island chain, and while it has plenty of vineyards, it is not nearly as cultivated as one of its neighboring islands.

INCORRECT.

Stromboli in the U.S. might be best known as a pizza-like turnover, but in Sicily, it is a famously temperamental volcanic island with frequent and explosive eruptions. In 2019, it did this. Good thing it’s also the most isolated of the main islands!

Campania Vine Training

What is the name of the unique vine training system employed for Agliancio grapes in the Taurasi DOCG and Irpinia province of Campania?

CORRECT.

Dating back centuries, this canopy vine-training system literally refers to the spokes of a wheel, for the vines are sent up a central stake then radiate outward across wires. This allows the vines to create a leaf canopy to protect the grapes, slow the maturation process down, and preserve acidity and control sugar development. Furthermore, the buds are better protected against frost by being higher off the ground. This method is partly why Taurasi has one of the latest harvests in all of Italy (its elevation has something to do with that, too). Why uproot them and "go guyot" if you’ve got a good thing going? Monstrous old raggiera vines can resemble giant trees, with some examples dating back 200 years.

INCORRECT.

Tendone, meaning “tent" is a high-volume canopy training system used across Italy, but more commonly in Puglia, Sicily and Abruzzo.

INCORRECT.

Alberata pertains to training vines into trees, a very ancient and variable method that is still used in isolated instances in Campania and Umbria.

INCORRECT.

Ventilatore is a made-up training system. Couldn’t help myself. But it kind of sounds like one that would exist, huh?

title: 9 Red Wines That Tell the Story of Modern Campania
summary:
A Recent Tasting Shows a Character Unlike Any Other in Italy

The post 9 Red Wines That Tell the Story of Modern Campania appeared first on Opening a Bottle.
content:
10 min read

This past April, I attended part of the annual media event known as Campania Stories in the city of Caserta. I’ve been meaning to get down to this corner of Italy for some time, a place whose energetic white wines and hearty reds I’ve admired for their tenacious quality. Appreciating them from afar is easy. But to understand why they are what they are? That takes a lot more in situ experience, which — sadly — two days at Campania Stories couldn’t possibly provide. Campania is massive, and whether they are tucked into the rolling hills of Irpinia or the urban sprawl of Naples, the region’s wineries are dramatically isolated from one another. A deeper dive requires a lot of time on the road.

The red wines of Campania have a raw tenacity to them that demands attention.

The visit may have been all-too-brief, but it did provide an intriguing glimpse at what’s happening with modern winemaking in the region. Because so much of what I tasted was of the red sort, I am going to focus there in this report.

Enjoy This Article Free Courtesy of Miriade & Partners

Miriade & Partners has used a benefit of their Wine Trade Group Subscription to unlock this article from our paywall 45 days after its publication as a gift to my readers. Thanks to them, and all of my paying members, for making this site possible.

Wine Trade Group Subscriptions

Wine Lover Membership

The Indigenous Reds

The red wines of Campania have a raw tenacity to them that demands attention. Some might call the style “rustic” or “unpolished,” but I don’t think that is fair. “Wild” or “unbridled” is a better descriptor, because much of this character is coming from the grape varieties themselves, not rough winemaking (which the former implies). Producers must appropriately nurture this energy without allowing that feral character to overwhelm the taster. Sometimes they don’t succeed, more often they do.

International grape varieties are virtually non-existent here. Aglianico rules, and Piedirosso is vying for attention. This latter grape is neatly positioned for modern tastes: it is mid-weight, fresh and with silky tannins, yet it easily conveys the smoky and earthy dimensions that are possible from a region rife with volcanic soil structures. Another contender for our attention is Casavecchia. Like Aglianico, it is big on tannins, but a bit less forceful and more color-rich thanks to its high anthocyanin count. If your palate gravitates to the berry patch, you’ll like its intrinsically fruity character, which is kept honest by intriguing floral and earthy tones.

Where to Look

Each of the wines profiled below are in limited supply and worth the hunt. While Terredora di Paolo, Mastroberardino, and Feudo di San Gregorio are missing from this report, they are the three major players that I’ve had the most consistent results from in the past, and are good choices if that’s what your market is limited to. Wines from Feudo di San Gregorio were featured in this tasting, but they weren’t quite up to the level of these wines featured below.

In short: I think Campania’s wild character is best shown by the indie artisans.

Navigate This Guide

Alphabetical

  • 2024 Cantine Olivella “VIPT” Vesuvio Piedirosso
  • 2025 Casa Setaro “Munazei” Lacryma di Christi del Vesuvio Rosso
  • 2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso
  • 2019 Fattoria di Rivolta “Simbiosi” Beneventano Rosso
  • 2019 Il Verro “Monte Maggiore” Terre del Volturno Casavecchia
  • 2022 Luigi Tecce “Satyricon” Campania Aglianico
  • 2022 Marisa Cuomo “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Furore Rosso Riserva
  • 2015 Perillo Taurasi
  • 2021 Torricino “Cevotiempo” Taurasi

Captions

My Favorites

Top Wine: 2015 Perillo Taurasi

           

I was thrilled to visit the Perillo estate in Taurasi as part of my visit. I love smaller, family-oriented producers, and seeing the wisdom of Michele Perillo passed down to his two young sons, Felice and Nico, was a potent reminder on what propels Italian wine forward more than anything: generational change.

I’ve added this fine winery to my curated list of Essential Winemakers of Italy, where you can learn more about the estate and its philosophy. Taurasi is best when it has aged at least 10 years, and this 2015 — which was exhibited at the Caserta tasting as a current release — is among the finest examples I’ve ever tasted. It draws its power from 100+ year old vines that grow at high elevation, and which are trained in the traditional raggiera method of the region (see photo at the right/bottom).

Drinkers of Barolo will take this wine’s finesse to heart, but the sanguine aromas and blood-orange citrus-like profile of its acidity is pure Aglianico. Slatey tannins and a wild, expansive persistence suggested to me that this wine might have another decade or two of life left to give. One of the best wines I’ve tasted all year.

Return to Wine List

Just Drink It: 2024 Cantine Olivella “VIPT” Vesuvio Piedirosso

       

Profiled in my recent article on Vesuvius, Cantine Olivella represents the other side of the Campania red wine spectrum from Perillo, and their Vesuvio Piedirosso called “VIPT” is the perfect emblem of fresher, spicier, more playful possibilities.

Piedirosso is an ancient local variety that has emerged in recent years as Campania’s No. 2 most important red grape. The “red foot” of its name harkens to its traditional moniker, Pèr e’ Palummo, or pigeon’s foot, which accurately describes the color of the grape’s stems. It offers some of the most generous berry-like flavors of any Italian grape, and when grown in a concentration of volcanic soil, it  shines with a nice endurance on the finish.

I particularly liked the lift of spice, the tinge of bitterness and the sentiment behind this wine (in local dialect, “vipt” means “drink it!”).

Return to Wine List

Quintessential Vesuvius: 2025 Casa Setaro “Munazei” Lacryma di Christi del Vesuvio Rosso

           

Some of the most exciting wines in Italy blend the spirit of ancient winemaking traditions with a knack for the demands of modern taste. For this dazzling Piedirosso, winemaker Massimo Setaro chose to name it “Munazei” after the historic sheds that kept fruits and vegetables fresh in the days before widespread refrigeration. It has the classic embrace of sour, sweet and bitter flavors that you really only find in wines from the Mediterranean, but also a playful verve that would fit right in at the trendiest wine bars in Manhattan, Tokyo and Copenhagen.

But the more I came back to this wine, the more I saw it as a true original. Grown on the lower slopes of Vesuvius a stone’s throw away from Pompeii, the wine I tasted was tinged with a mineral, smoky character that propelled my intrigue more and more. I was reminded of cherries, violets, almonds and spice.

Return to Wine List

The Survivor: 2019 Il Verro “Monte Maggiore” Terre del Volturno Casavecchia

         

One of the most persistent narratives in Italian wine is the local grape variety saved from the brink of extinction by a dogged producer. Friuli has Ronchi di Cialla and Schioppettino, Piedmont has Walter Massa and Timorasso, and Marche and Abruzzo can tip their cap to Guido Cocci Grifoni for saving Pecorino. But what about Campania? In a region as vast, mountainous and often undeveloped as this one, surely some grape has been hiding in plain sight?

Indeed, there is not one but many in Campania. My recent profile on Vesuvius focused on two: Catalanesca and Caprettone. But in the northern woods of the region, tucked away in a historic hunting preserve where wild boar outnumber humans, you’ll find the estate of Il Verro, where the philosophy is twofold: organic wine production + forgotten indigenous grapes. Alongside Coda di Pecora, and Pallagrello Nero and Bianco, you’ll find Casavecchia, a grape whose name underscores its singularity. The local folktale refers to the early 1900s when a large trunk of an unknown grapevine was discovered by a dilapidated old house.

The flavor profile of this wine is completely different from Aglianico and Piedirosso. Its more generous body and velvet-like tannins feel like a major mood shift from Taurasi’s rock-and-roll and Vesuvio’s acid jazz. You might be reminded of plums, berries and dried orange peel when you dip your nose below the rim. And while that may sound like a softer, more gentler experience, this Casavecchia suggests that the wine is no wallflower. I’d expect it to improve with age and be able to handle heartier food pairings if you so desire.

Return to Wine List

Honorable Mentions

2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso

     

Contrada Salandra lies to the west of Naples near the series of craters that comprise the “super volcano” of Campi Flegrei. Giuseppe and Sandra Fortunato have always produced wine with an ecological mindset (Sandra was a beekeeper before she took up wine), and their blurry bee wine label is one of the most recognizable in Campania. I’ve long adored this wine, and it was nice to see the 2022 showing so well. It offered compelling aromas akin to orange citrus and a cigar box, with a kinetic energy I found to be irresistible.

Return to Wine List

2019 Fattoria di Rivolta “Simbiosi” Beneventano Rosso

         

With Aglianico and Piedirosso representing two important — by stylistically distinct — anchor points on the Campania wine horizon, it would seem natural to ask “what happens when you blend them together?” I tasted a few such blends, but Fattoria di Rivolta’s “Simbiosi” revealed the most alchemy between the two. The aromas of cherry and truffle as well as firm tannins reminded me quite a bit of Nebbiolo, but it was the softer sense of acidity that lent this wine a unique voice. Interesting, the soil at Fattoria di Rivolta in Benevento leans more calcareous clay, which likely accounts for the slightly mellower sense of energy in this wine.

Return to Wine List

2022 Marisa Cuomo “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Furore Rosso Riserva

         

There is no scene more closely associated with Campania (with Italy, in fact) than the Amalfi Coast. Comprised of dolomitic limestone cliffs and dripping with colorful, compact villages interspersed with lemon groves and vineyards, it is the icon of Italian idylls. But the volume of wine from this Mediterranean paradise is minuscule. The vines have to be trained on pergolas, terraces are steep and narrow, and everything has to be done by hand. As big as the Amalfi Coast “brand” is, wines from here will always be rare and costly.

Fortunately, they’re delicious, especially in the hands of the coastline’s most famous producer, Marisa Cuomo. The “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Rosso Riserva is yet another blend of Aglianico and Piedirosso, but unlike Fattoria di Rivolta’s “Simbiosi,” which leans heavily on Aglianico, this one is 50-50. It also comes from very old vines that grow some 600 to 1,800 feet above the Tyrrhenian Sea. The wine is supple and showcases aromas and flavors that might remind you of pomegranates or currants. Delicate floral and nutty tones counter everything to reveal a graceful arch that marries well with a variety of cuisines.

Return to Wine List

2022 Luigi Tecce “Satyricon” Campania Aglianico

       

Luigi Tecce is the Jackson Pollack of Italian wine. His wines are singular acts of non-conformity, yet nothing about them feels planned or sculpted. They are what they are, even if that means challenging. In my book, Opening a Bottle: Italy, I included Tecce’s iconic Taurasi Riserva called “Poliphemo” as one of the 100 Wines to Admire. “Some wines want to be loved,” I wrote. “Luigi Tecce’s ‘Poliphemo’ is not one of those wines.”

While his famously hands-off approach is not for everyone, there is something undeniably real and authentic about what they convey in the glass. And this year, it was his “lightest” and “most youthful” Aglianico — “Satyricon” — that most caught my attention. I put those adjectives in quotes because they deserve some context: this wine is still explosively intense with those savory and smoky traits best known in Tecce’s Taurasi. But I found everything to be in better balance here. Undeniably age-worthy and collectible, I wouldn’t complain about its Barolo-like price at all. It’s worth it.

Return to Wine List

2021 Torricino “Cevotiempo” Taurasi

       

I’d be remiss to exclude a more classically etched yet modern Taurasi in this report, since that’s the style that largely dominates the DOCG. If Luigi Tecce’s Taurasi wines are adventurous escapades, Torricino’s are like a comfortable evening in the backyard. That said, “Cevotiempo” needs time, as the name suggests. The 2021, even with five years of age, is still fairly coiled, but what’s residing inside its core is a brilliant demonstration of Aglianico’s sophistication. Tinged with dried herbal notes and polished tannins, the wine’s acidity is carried forward by an intriguing sensation of salinity that begs for another sip.

Return to Wine List

Captions

From top to bottom (All photos ©Kevin Day for Opening a Bottle):

  • Bottle of 2015 Perillo Taurasi.
  • The first buds of the season on raggiera-trained Aglianico vines of Perillo in the Taurasi DOCG.
  • Aglianico in the glass.
  • A mixed vineyard with ample Aglianico and Piedirosso beneath Vesuvius at Casa Setaro.
  • The Perillo family of Taurasi: sons Nico and Felice (left and right), with father, winemaker Michele Perillo (center).
  • Piedirosso in the glass.
  • Bottle of 2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso.
  • The wines of Luigi Tecce.
  • A rose blooming in the vineyards of Cantine Olivella.

Dating back centuries, this canopy vine-training system literally refers to the spokes of a wheel, for the vines are sent up a central stake then radiate outward across wires. This allows the vines to create a leaf canopy to protect the grapes, slow the maturation process down, and preserve acidity and control sugar development. Furthermore, the buds are better protected against frost by being higher off the ground. This method is partly why Taurasi has one of the latest harvests in all of Italy (its elevation has something to do with that, too). Why uproot them and "go guyot" if you’ve got a good thing going? Monstrous old raggiera vines can resemble giant trees, with some examples dating back 200 years.

INCORRECT.

Tendone, meaning “tent" is a high-volume canopy training system used across Italy, but more commonly in Puglia, Sicily and Abruzzo.

INCORRECT.

Alberata pertains to training vines into trees, a very ancient and variable method that is still used in isolated instances in Campania and Umbria.

INCORRECT.

Ventilatore is a made-up training system. Couldn’t help myself. But it kind of sounds like one that would exist, huh?

title: 9 Red Wines That Tell the Story of Modern Campania
summary:
A Recent Tasting Shows a Character Unlike Any Other in Italy

The post 9 Red Wines That Tell the Story of Modern Campania appeared first on Opening a Bottle.
content:
10 min read

This past April, I attended part of the annual media event known as Campania Stories in the city of Caserta. I’ve been meaning to get down to this corner of Italy for some time, a place whose energetic white wines and hearty reds I’ve admired for their tenacious quality. Appreciating them from afar is easy. But to understand why they are what they are? That takes a lot more in situ experience, which — sadly — two days at Campania Stories couldn’t possibly provide. Campania is massive, and whether they are tucked into the rolling hills of Irpinia or the urban sprawl of Naples, the region’s wineries are dramatically isolated from one another. A deeper dive requires a lot of time on the road.

The red wines of Campania have a raw tenacity to them that demands attention.

The visit may have been all-too-brief, but it did provide an intriguing glimpse at what’s happening with modern winemaking in the region. Because so much of what I tasted was of the red sort, I am going to focus there in this report.

Enjoy This Article Free Courtesy of Miriade & Partners

Miriade & Partners has used a benefit of their Wine Trade Group Subscription to unlock this article from our paywall 45 days after its publication as a gift to my readers. Thanks to them, and all of my paying members, for making this site possible.

Wine Trade Group Subscriptions

Wine Lover Membership

The Indigenous Reds

The red wines of Campania have a raw tenacity to them that demands attention. Some might call the style “rustic” or “unpolished,” but I don’t think that is fair. “Wild” or “unbridled” is a better descriptor, because much of this character is coming from the grape varieties themselves, not rough winemaking (which the former implies). Producers must appropriately nurture this energy without allowing that feral character to overwhelm the taster. Sometimes they don’t succeed, more often they do.

International grape varieties are virtually non-existent here. Aglianico rules, and Piedirosso is vying for attention. This latter grape is neatly positioned for modern tastes: it is mid-weight, fresh and with silky tannins, yet it easily conveys the smoky and earthy dimensions that are possible from a region rife with volcanic soil structures. Another contender for our attention is Casavecchia. Like Aglianico, it is big on tannins, but a bit less forceful and more color-rich thanks to its high anthocyanin count. If your palate gravitates to the berry patch, you’ll like its intrinsically fruity character, which is kept honest by intriguing floral and earthy tones.

Where to Look

Each of the wines profiled below are in limited supply and worth the hunt. While Terredora di Paolo, Mastroberardino, and Feudo di San Gregorio are missing from this report, they are the three major players that I’ve had the most consistent results from in the past, and are good choices if that’s what your market is limited to. Wines from Feudo di San Gregorio were featured in this tasting, but they weren’t quite up to the level of these wines featured below.

In short: I think Campania’s wild character is best shown by the indie artisans.

Navigate This Guide

Alphabetical

  • 2024 Cantine Olivella “VIPT” Vesuvio Piedirosso
  • 2025 Casa Setaro “Munazei” Lacryma di Christi del Vesuvio Rosso
  • 2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso
  • 2019 Fattoria di Rivolta “Simbiosi” Beneventano Rosso
  • 2019 Il Verro “Monte Maggiore” Terre del Volturno Casavecchia
  • 2022 Luigi Tecce “Satyricon” Campania Aglianico
  • 2022 Marisa Cuomo “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Furore Rosso Riserva
  • 2015 Perillo Taurasi
  • 2021 Torricino “Cevotiempo” Taurasi

Captions

My Favorites

Top Wine: 2015 Perillo Taurasi

           

I was thrilled to visit the Perillo estate in Taurasi as part of my visit. I love smaller, family-oriented producers, and seeing the wisdom of Michele Perillo passed down to his two young sons, Felice and Nico, was a potent reminder on what propels Italian wine forward more than anything: generational change.

I’ve added this fine winery to my curated list of Essential Winemakers of Italy, where you can learn more about the estate and its philosophy. Taurasi is best when it has aged at least 10 years, and this 2015 — which was exhibited at the Caserta tasting as a current release — is among the finest examples I’ve ever tasted. It draws its power from 100+ year old vines that grow at high elevation, and which are trained in the traditional raggiera method of the region (see photo at the right/bottom).

Drinkers of Barolo will take this wine’s finesse to heart, but the sanguine aromas and blood-orange citrus-like profile of its acidity is pure Aglianico. Slatey tannins and a wild, expansive persistence suggested to me that this wine might have another decade or two of life left to give. One of the best wines I’ve tasted all year.

Return to Wine List

Just Drink It: 2024 Cantine Olivella “VIPT” Vesuvio Piedirosso

       

Profiled in my recent article on Vesuvius, Cantine Olivella represents the other side of the Campania red wine spectrum from Perillo, and their Vesuvio Piedirosso called “VIPT” is the perfect emblem of fresher, spicier, more playful possibilities.

Piedirosso is an ancient local variety that has emerged in recent years as Campania’s No. 2 most important red grape. The “red foot” of its name harkens to its traditional moniker, Pèr e’ Palummo, or pigeon’s foot, which accurately describes the color of the grape’s stems. It offers some of the most generous berry-like flavors of any Italian grape, and when grown in a concentration of volcanic soil, it  shines with a nice endurance on the finish.

I particularly liked the lift of spice, the tinge of bitterness and the sentiment behind this wine (in local dialect, “vipt” means “drink it!”).

Return to Wine List

Quintessential Vesuvius: 2025 Casa Setaro “Munazei” Lacryma di Christi del Vesuvio Rosso

           

Some of the most exciting wines in Italy blend the spirit of ancient winemaking traditions with a knack for the demands of modern taste. For this dazzling Piedirosso, winemaker Massimo Setaro chose to name it “Munazei” after the historic sheds that kept fruits and vegetables fresh in the days before widespread refrigeration. It has the classic embrace of sour, sweet and bitter flavors that you really only find in wines from the Mediterranean, but also a playful verve that would fit right in at the trendiest wine bars in Manhattan, Tokyo and Copenhagen.

But the more I came back to this wine, the more I saw it as a true original. Grown on the lower slopes of Vesuvius a stone’s throw away from Pompeii, the wine I tasted was tinged with a mineral, smoky character that propelled my intrigue more and more. I was reminded of cherries, violets, almonds and spice.

Return to Wine List

The Survivor: 2019 Il Verro “Monte Maggiore” Terre del Volturno Casavecchia

         

One of the most persistent narratives in Italian wine is the local grape variety saved from the brink of extinction by a dogged producer. Friuli has Ronchi di Cialla and Schioppettino, Piedmont has Walter Massa and Timorasso, and Marche and Abruzzo can tip their cap to Guido Cocci Grifoni for saving Pecorino. But what about Campania? In a region as vast, mountainous and often undeveloped as this one, surely some grape has been hiding in plain sight?

Indeed, there is not one but many in Campania. My recent profile on Vesuvius focused on two: Catalanesca and Caprettone. But in the northern woods of the region, tucked away in a historic hunting preserve where wild boar outnumber humans, you’ll find the estate of Il Verro, where the philosophy is twofold: organic wine production + forgotten indigenous grapes. Alongside Coda di Pecora, and Pallagrello Nero and Bianco, you’ll find Casavecchia, a grape whose name underscores its singularity. The local folktale refers to the early 1900s when a large trunk of an unknown grapevine was discovered by a dilapidated old house.

The flavor profile of this wine is completely different from Aglianico and Piedirosso. Its more generous body and velvet-like tannins feel like a major mood shift from Taurasi’s rock-and-roll and Vesuvio’s acid jazz. You might be reminded of plums, berries and dried orange peel when you dip your nose below the rim. And while that may sound like a softer, more gentler experience, this Casavecchia suggests that the wine is no wallflower. I’d expect it to improve with age and be able to handle heartier food pairings if you so desire.

Return to Wine List

Honorable Mentions

2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso

     

Contrada Salandra lies to the west of Naples near the series of craters that comprise the “super volcano” of Campi Flegrei. Giuseppe and Sandra Fortunato have always produced wine with an ecological mindset (Sandra was a beekeeper before she took up wine), and their blurry bee wine label is one of the most recognizable in Campania. I’ve long adored this wine, and it was nice to see the 2022 showing so well. It offered compelling aromas akin to orange citrus and a cigar box, with a kinetic energy I found to be irresistible.

Return to Wine List

2019 Fattoria di Rivolta “Simbiosi” Beneventano Rosso

         

With Aglianico and Piedirosso representing two important — by stylistically distinct — anchor points on the Campania wine horizon, it would seem natural to ask “what happens when you blend them together?” I tasted a few such blends, but Fattoria di Rivolta’s “Simbiosi” revealed the most alchemy between the two. The aromas of cherry and truffle as well as firm tannins reminded me quite a bit of Nebbiolo, but it was the softer sense of acidity that lent this wine a unique voice. Interesting, the soil at Fattoria di Rivolta in Benevento leans more calcareous clay, which likely accounts for the slightly mellower sense of energy in this wine.

Return to Wine List

2022 Marisa Cuomo “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Furore Rosso Riserva

         

There is no scene more closely associated with Campania (with Italy, in fact) than the Amalfi Coast. Comprised of dolomitic limestone cliffs and dripping with colorful, compact villages interspersed with lemon groves and vineyards, it is the icon of Italian idylls. But the volume of wine from this Mediterranean paradise is minuscule. The vines have to be trained on pergolas, terraces are steep and narrow, and everything has to be done by hand. As big as the Amalfi Coast “brand” is, wines from here will always be rare and costly.

Fortunately, they’re delicious, especially in the hands of the coastline’s most famous producer, Marisa Cuomo. The “Furore” Costa d’Amalfi Rosso Riserva is yet another blend of Aglianico and Piedirosso, but unlike Fattoria di Rivolta’s “Simbiosi,” which leans heavily on Aglianico, this one is 50-50. It also comes from very old vines that grow some 600 to 1,800 feet above the Tyrrhenian Sea. The wine is supple and showcases aromas and flavors that might remind you of pomegranates or currants. Delicate floral and nutty tones counter everything to reveal a graceful arch that marries well with a variety of cuisines.

Return to Wine List

2022 Luigi Tecce “Satyricon” Campania Aglianico

       

Luigi Tecce is the Jackson Pollack of Italian wine. His wines are singular acts of non-conformity, yet nothing about them feels planned or sculpted. They are what they are, even if that means challenging. In my book, Opening a Bottle: Italy, I included Tecce’s iconic Taurasi Riserva called “Poliphemo” as one of the 100 Wines to Admire. “Some wines want to be loved,” I wrote. “Luigi Tecce’s ‘Poliphemo’ is not one of those wines.”

While his famously hands-off approach is not for everyone, there is something undeniably real and authentic about what they convey in the glass. And this year, it was his “lightest” and “most youthful” Aglianico — “Satyricon” — that most caught my attention. I put those adjectives in quotes because they deserve some context: this wine is still explosively intense with those savory and smoky traits best known in Tecce’s Taurasi. But I found everything to be in better balance here. Undeniably age-worthy and collectible, I wouldn’t complain about its Barolo-like price at all. It’s worth it.

Return to Wine List

2021 Torricino “Cevotiempo” Taurasi

       

I’d be remiss to exclude a more classically etched yet modern Taurasi in this report, since that’s the style that largely dominates the DOCG. If Luigi Tecce’s Taurasi wines are adventurous escapades, Torricino’s are like a comfortable evening in the backyard. That said, “Cevotiempo” needs time, as the name suggests. The 2021, even with five years of age, is still fairly coiled, but what’s residing inside its core is a brilliant demonstration of Aglianico’s sophistication. Tinged with dried herbal notes and polished tannins, the wine’s acidity is carried forward by an intriguing sensation of salinity that begs for another sip.

Return to Wine List

  • The first buds of the season on raggiera-trained Aglianico vines of Perillo in the Taurasi DOCG.
  • Aglianico in the glass.
  • A mixed vineyard with ample Aglianico and Piedirosso beneath Vesuvius at Casa Setaro.
  • The Perillo family of Taurasi: sons Nico and Felice (left and right), with father, winemaker Michele Perillo (center).
  • Piedirosso in the glass.
  • Bottle of 2022 Contrada Salandra Campi Flegrei Piedirosso.
  • The wines of Luigi Tecce.
  • A rose blooming in the vineyards of Cantine Olivella.
